Chapter 1 · Origins · c. 3000 a. C.–500 a. C.

The first questions about mind and behaviour

Long before the word "psychology" existed, people were already asking about dreams, madness, memory and character.

Psychology as a discipline is little more than a century old, but its questions are as old as writing. Why do we dream? Why does someone lose their reason? Where is the thing that makes us who we are? The first answers mixed gods, spirits and very precise observations of the body.

What were people trying to understand?

Above all, what was out of the ordinary: seizures, delusions, sudden changes in behaviour and dreams, which many cultures read as messages. Everyday matters also mattered: how to raise children, how to control anger, how to advise a ruler. Egyptian wisdom texts such as the Instructions of Ptahhotep are, at heart, manuals of conduct and of dealing with others.

With what methods?

Direct observation, oral tradition and medical practice. In Mesopotamia long lists of symptoms and their prognosis were compiled, and they include conditions we would now call epilepsy or mood disorders, almost always attributed to demons or to the hand of a god. Egyptian and Babylonian "dream books" listed typical dreams and their meaning.

One of the most striking documents is the Edwin Smith papyrus, copied around 1600 BCE from older texts. It describes 48 cases of injury, several of them to the head, in a surprisingly practical tone. It contains the earliest known written description of the brain and links skull injuries to paralysis on one side of the body, without resorting to magical explanations in those cases.

Who took part?

Priests, scribes, physicians and healers whose names we almost never know. In many parts of the world, from Neolithic Europe to the Andes, people practised trepanation: cutting a hole in the skull of a living person. Skulls with regrown bone show that many survived. We do not know for sure why it was done: perhaps to treat wounds, headaches or seizures, perhaps for ritual reasons.

What did it contribute?

  • The idea that behaviour and mood can be disturbed and can therefore be observed and described.
  • The first classifications of symptoms, joining what we would now separate into medicine and psychology.
  • A link, still vague, between the head and functions such as movement and speech.

What was revised later?

For many people the heart remained the seat of thought and emotion for centuries; the Egyptians preserved the heart of mummies and discarded the brain. Supernatural explanations lived alongside natural ones for millennia, and the separation between them was slow and uneven. It also pays to be careful when reading these texts with modern eyes: giving modern names to ancient symptoms is tempting but often misleading.

The first answers were very different from ours, but the questions were already the same.

  1. Breasted, J. H. (1930). The Edwin Smith Surgical Papyrus. Chicago: University of Chicago Press.
